A dune is a hill or mound of loose sand that has been built and shaped entirely by wind.

That's the core of it. But to truly understand dunes, you need to understand how they form, what they look like, how they behave, and where they appear — so let's go through each one.
How a dune forms

Wind is the engine behind every dune. When wind blows across open ground covered in loose sand, it picks up individual sand grains and carries them forward. When the wind slows down — because of an obstacle like a rock, a clump of grass, or just a shift in terrain — it drops those grains. They pile up. More wind brings more sand, and the pile grows taller and wider over time. That's a dune being born.
What a dune looks like

<br>
A typical dune has two sides that look completely different from each other:

  • The windward side (the side the wind blows against) is gentle and slopes gradually upward. Wind pushes sand grains up this side slowly.
  • The slip face (the sheltered side, away from the wind) is steep. When sand grains reach the peak — called the crest — they tumble and slide down this steeper side.

<br>
This lopsided shape is one of the most reliable signs you're looking at a dune, not just any random sand hill.

Dunes move — and this surprises most people

<br>
Dunes are not stationary. Because sand is constantly being pushed up the windward side and deposited on the slip face, the entire dune gradually migrates in the direction the wind blows. A dune can slowly creep across a landscape over weeks, months, or years — burying whatever lies in its path. In some deserts, entire roads, villages, and ancient ruins have been swallowed by migrating dunes.
Types of dunes

Not all dunes look the same. Their shape is determined by wind direction, how consistent the wind is, and how much sand is available.
<br>
<br>
Barchan dunes are crescent-shaped, with two "arms" pointing in the direction the wind blows. They form where there's a steady wind and a limited sand supply.
<br>
<br>
<br>
<br>

Transverse dunes are long, wave-like ridges running perpendicular to the wind — like ocean waves frozen in sand. They appear where there's an abundant sand supply and a consistent wind direction.
<br>
<br>
<br>
<br>
<br>
<br>

Star dunes have multiple ridges radiating outward from a tall central peak, like a star when seen from above. They form where winds blow from several different directions and can grow extraordinarily tall.
<br>
<br>
<br>
<br>
<br>

Longitudinal dunes (also called seif dunes) are long, parallel ridges that run in the same direction as the wind. They can stretch for kilometers across a desert.
<br>
<br>
Parabolic dunes are U-shaped, with the opening facing into the wind — essentially a reversed barchan. They're common near coastlines, where patches of vegetation anchor parts of the sand and hold the "arms" in place while the middle blows forward.
Where dunes are found

The most famous dunes are in deserts. The Sahara in Africa and the Arabian Desert in the Middle East are home to some of the most dramatic dune landscapes on Earth. But dunes are not exclusive to deserts. They also form:

  • On beaches, where coastal winds shape sand near the shoreline. These are often called coastal dunes or beach dunes. They tend to be smaller and are very common worldwide.
  • Along riverbeds and lakeshores, where dried sediment is exposed to wind.
  • In cold and polar regions, where strong winds pile up fine sand deposited by ancient glaciers.
  • On other planets — Mars has enormous dune fields visible from space, and dunes have been found on Saturn's moon Titan as well.
Size

Dunes range enormously in scale. A small coastal dune might only come up to your knee, while the largest desert dunes can exceed 300 metres in height — taller than the Eiffel Tower. The tallest dunes in the world are found in the Badain Jaran Desert in China and in certain parts of the Sahara.
Dunes and sound

Some dunes produce a deep, low rumbling or humming sound — almost like a distant engine or a musical note — when sand avalanches down the slip face. These are called singing dunes or booming dunes. The sound happens because millions of sand grains vibrating together create a resonance. It can last for several minutes and be heard from kilometres away. The phenomenon has been recorded on multiple continents and puzzled scientists for centuries.
Dunes and life

Despite looking lifeless, dunes can support entire ecosystems. Coastal dunes are often colonized by specialised grasses — such as marram grass — whose deep, spreading roots bind the sand and stabilize the dune, preventing it from wandering. Desert dunes support insects, lizards, snakes, small mammals like the fennec fox, and even plants adapted to growing in loose, shifting sand. Some desert plants send roots down several metres to reach groundwater beneath the dune.
One important distinction

People sometimes use "dune" loosely for any sandy mound near water, and that's fine — those are still dunes, because wind still formed them. But the key thing that makes something a dune is wind action. A pile of sand dumped by a river, or a sandbar shaped by water currents, is not a dune. Wind is the defining ingredient. If wind didn't build it, it isn't a dune.
